```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r attach}
library(mysterymodel)
```

This is the whole pipeline on one cohort, in the order it has to run: say what
is being predicted, account for every row that leaves, describe what is left,
fit, validate on a stated basis, and draw an instrument that is checked against
the model rather than assumed to match it.

Every number below comes from synthetic data. The package carries no patient
data and never will, so `mm_synthetic_cohort()` is what the examples, the
fixtures and the articles all run on.

## A cohort with known truth

```{r cohort}
raw <- mm_synthetic_cohort(n = 500, prevalence = 0.11, seed = 1978)
str(raw, give.attr = FALSE)
attr(raw, "truth")$formula
```

The generating model is deliberately not additive. It carries a quadratic age
effect and one `prior_uti` by `sex` interaction, because a pipeline exercised
only on additive data never reveals whether its spline and hierarchy handling
are right. The `truth` attribute is what later sections are checked against.

About 8% of rows are a second visit by a patient already present, which is what
`pid` is for:

```{r repeats}
sum(duplicated(raw$pid))
```

The generator produces complete data and a real export does not, so a little
missingness goes in deliberately. Everything downstream has to cope with it,
and a vignette on complete data would not show whether it does.

```{r holes}
set.seed(4)
raw$bmi[sample(nrow(raw), 9)] <- NA
raw$indication[sample(nrow(raw), 6)] <- NA
```

## Describe what was exported, before deciding who is eligible

```{r eda}
desc <- mm_eda(raw, by = "event",
               vars = c("age", "bmi", "sex", "prior_uti", "indication"))
desc$table
```

The missing count sits beside each variable rather than in a separate table,
because a percentage whose denominator quietly excludes missing rows reads as a
fact about the cohort when it is a fact about the rows that happened to be
complete. The denominator each percentage was taken over is the first row.

```{r missing}
desc$missing
desc$duplicates
```

This is a data frame, not a rendered table. `gt`, `gtsummary`,
`knitr::kable()` and Quarto can all render it, and none of them is needed to
compute it.

The cells are strings because the formatting is part of the contract: counts
with thousands separators, percentages to one decimal, means with standard
deviations, medians with the quartiles. The same four helpers build every cell,
so a table cannot be internally inconsistent about how it rounds:

```{r formatters}
c(mysterymodel:::mm_count(12345),
  mysterymodel:::mm_n_pct(45, 404),
  mysterymodel:::mm_mean_sd(raw$age),
  mysterymodel:::mm_median_iqr(raw$age))
```

## Eligibility, with a ledger that reconciles

Each rule is a named one-sided formula. The name is what a flow diagram will
say, so it should read as the criterion it expresses.

```{r clean}
cohort <- mm_clean(raw, rules = list(
  "aged 40 or over"     = ~ age >= 40,
  "plausible BMI"       = ~ bmi >= 16 & bmi <= 55,
  "indication recorded" = ~ !is.na(indication)
), label = "urodynamics studies as exported")

cohort
```

Rows in must equal rows out plus every exclusion. `mm_clean()` errors rather
than returning a cohort it cannot reconcile, which is the one thing it exists
to prevent:

```{r ledger}
cohort$ledger[, c("rule", "n_excluded", "n_after", "reason")]
c(in_ = cohort$n_in, out = cohort$n_out, excluded = cohort$n_excluded)
```

Look at the two `plausible BMI` lines. Nine rows have no BMI, so the rule is
neither true nor false for them, and they leave under their own heading rather
than passing. A rule that evaluates to `NA` is not a pass: treating unknown
eligibility as eligible and treating it as ineligible are different studies,
and the difference belongs in the diagram.

The cohort that goes on to be modelled is complete by construction, because
the rules above made completeness a stated eligibility criterion rather than a
side effect of whatever the fitting function drops:

```{r complete}
mm_eda(cohort, vars = c("age", "bmi", "sex", "prior_uti",
                        "indication"))$missing
```

Imputation instead of exclusion is a v0.3 item. Until it exists, the exclusion
is visible in the ledger, which is the honest version of the same decision.

## The plan, written down before anything is fitted

```{r project}
project <- mm_project(
  slug           = "uds",
  outcome        = "event",
  predictors     = c("age", "bmi", "sex", "prior_uti", "indication"),
  positive_class = 1,
  cohort         = cohort$data,
  split_var      = "year",
  split_at       = 2023,
  cluster_id     = "pid",
  seed           = 1978
)

project
```

Nothing is fitted here. The point of the object is that a reviewer can check it
against the protocol instead of reconstructing it afterwards from whichever
code ran. It fails closed on configurations that cannot be meant:

```{r fail-closed, error = TRUE}
mm_project("uds", "event", c("age", "event"))

mm_project("uds", "event", c("age", "bmi"), split_var = "year")

mm_project("uds", "event", c("age", "bmi"),
           positive_class = "yes", cohort = cohort$data)
```

The third is worth dwelling on. An inverted positive class inverts every risk
the model goes on to report, and nothing downstream looks wrong.

## Fit

```{r model}
model <- mm_model(project, cohort$data,
                  nonlinear    = "age",
                  interactions = list(c("prior_uti", "sex")),
                  knots        = 4)

model
```

The warning is the sample-size gate, and it is the honest answer for a cohort
this size. The gate is the Riley requirement from `pmsampsize`, not the
events-per-parameter rule, which is reported as description and labelled as
such:

```{r adequacy}
model$adequacy
```

Two independent routes agree. The heuristic shrinkage above is computed from
the likelihood ratio and the parameter count; the bootstrap calibration slopes
in the validation section below are estimated by resampling. The two land within
a few hundredths of each other, and neither calculation knows about the other.

Strong hierarchy is enforced before a formula exists, because a formula is the
last place to find out:

```{r hierarchy, error = TRUE}
mm_model(mm_project("uds", "event", c("age", "sex")), cohort$data,
         interactions = list(c("sex", "prior_uti")))
```

What was fitted, and what a deployed prediction is allowed to receive:

```{r schema}
deparse1(model$formula)
model$schema$predictors$sex
model$schema$predictors$age
model$fingerprint
```

## Predict

```{r predict}
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(58, 71, 103),
  bmi        = c(24.0, 33.5, 28.0),
  sex        = factor(c("female", "male", "female")),
  prior_uti  = factor(c("no", "yes", "no"), levels = c("no", "yes")),
  indication = factor(c("incontinence", "retention", "prolapse"))
)

mm_predict(model, patients)
```

The third patient is 103 years old, beyond anything the model was developed on.
That row is scored, because refusing it would be its own kind of dishonesty,
but it is labelled rather than silently equated with interpolation.

A level the model never saw is a different matter, and is refused by name:

```{r unseen, error = TRUE}
odd <- patients[1, ]
odd$indication <- "urgency"
mm_predict(model, odd)
```

`rms` would fail inside `predictrms()` without naming the variable or the
level. A missing predictor is refused too, unless the caller says what to do
with it:

```{r missing-pred, error = TRUE}
gap <- patients[1, ]
gap$bmi <- NA
mm_predict(model, gap)
```

```{r missing-na}
mm_predict(model, gap, on_missing = "na")
```

## Validate, on a stated basis

```{r validate}
validation <- mm_validate(model, cohort$data, B = 100, full_process = TRUE)
validation
```

One row per basis, because the three numbers a clinical prediction paper
reports are not interchangeable, and presenting one as another is the
commonest way a published model flatters itself. The `glm.fit` warnings come
from the calibration slope in resamples where the predictions separate the
outcome; a cohort with 32 events throws them, and suppressing them would hide
exactly the instability the sample-size gate just warned about.

The held-out row is the one to report, and it is sobering: 18 events support a
c-statistic whose interval runs from 0.42 to 0.74. That is what a held-out
sample this size can tell you, and the interval is in the table so that nobody
has to take the point estimate on its own.

```{r metrics}
validation$metrics[, c("basis", "n", "events", "c_stat", "cal_slope")]
```

The `note` column is where each row says what produced it:

```{r notes}
cat(paste0("* ", validation$metrics$basis, ": ",
           validation$metrics$note, collapse = "\n"))
```

The next article takes these four rows apart.

## A nomogram that is checked against its model

```{r nomogram}
nom <- mm_nomogram(model, out_dir = NULL)
nom
```

`mm_nomogram()` reads the drawn nomogram back the way a clinician reads it,
summing points across axes and interpolating the printed linear predictor
scale, without consulting the fit. Then it refuses to return if the answer
disagrees with `mm_predict()`. A nomogram that disagrees with the model it was
drawn from is worse than no nomogram, because it is a published instrument
giving wrong risks.

```{r nomogram-plot, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 6.5}
plot(nom$nomogram)
```

Passing `out_dir` writes the PDF, and the SVG and PNG when `svglite` and `ragg`
are installed. The third article reads this nomogram back by hand.

## What is not here yet

Imputation inside resampling, the flexible calibration curve, selection,
collinearity reporting and the Quarto manuscript. The roadmap in the README
says which version each belongs to. The pipeline above is honest about its own
limits in the place it would be easiest to hide them, which is the `note`
column of the validation table.
